findings.explanation: The payback table behind 'wait for one to fail' is CEE's Minnesota study of homes without gas (propane furnace baseline, $329-$654/yr savings vs a propane furnace), not gas-heated homes; for gas homes RMI finds switching pays only when the furnace and AC must be replaced simultaneously, otherwise it costs more or saves too little, and Wilson's 55% is already computed against like-for-like replacement at end of life. Even in CEE's own table a single failure leaves 13-17 years against a condensing furnace. The corpus does not establish that a gas home usually comes out ahead by waiting for one unit to fail.
findings.suggestion: Say what the evidence supports for gas: if both work and you heat with gas, the models here mostly say switching now will not pay on bills, and even at replacement it paid in RMI's model only when the furnace and AC were replaced together.

findings.explanation: Wilson's unsubsidized NPV is against a reference of like-for-like replacement of the existing equipment at end of life (incremental cost over new reference equipment), so the 55%/59% shares are already the replacement-time case. findings.suggestion: Add 'compared with replacing the old equipment with the same kind when it wears out', and adjust the timing section so it does not imply the national figures would rise at replacement.

The models disagree on oil; the viewer hears only the loss. 'Oil heat is expensive' is also an uncovered factual claim (no assertion, no passage), and Cadmus shows oil can be the cheaper fuel on very cold days.
findings.suggestion: Say the models split on oil: the national lab model has most oil homes coming out ahead with a basic unit, while Deetjen's has most losing money, in part because most oil homes are in cold climates. Drop 'Oil heat is expensive' or cover it.

findings.explanation: 'In one group of homes' fixes the rev 1 finding. But 'let a smaller, more efficient heat pump do the job' can be heard as insulation letting the homeowner choose a more efficient unit; the passage says the medium- and high-efficiency units already modelled could be smaller ($4,000 and $2,500 lower installed cost), not that insulating enables a more efficient one.

findings.explanation: The unsupported cold/warm clause is gone and the sentence is accurate. But in a section on 'things that move these numbers' the viewer hears only that insulating raised upfront cost. The same study finds envelope upgrades cut the share of homes with higher bills from 39% to 19% with minimum-efficiency units (L362-L363) and slightly raise the positive-NPV share in cold climates while lowering it in warmer ones (L526-L529). Neither passage is in the package; without them the section reads as 'insulation makes the numbers worse'.
findings.suggestion: Record L362-L363 and L526-L529 through record-sources and add that insulating first cut the number of homes with higher bills and helped slightly in cold climates; or end the section without implying a verdict on payback.

findings.explanation: The first clause (switching a working gas system early is worse than anything the models priced) follows a fortiori from their replacement-time baseline and is fine. But 'even at replacement time they found gas homes rarely came out ahead' attributes Deetjen's 'rarely produces a benefit' (the only passage cited, L646-L654) to both models. The national lab model found the opposite for a large group: its positive-NPV group for the minimum-efficiency unit 'also [includes] most homes that use natural gas and have central AC in warmer climates' (L497-L503), the same passage s29 relies on for oil, and s25 has 38-99% of gas homes with AC saving on bills. A gas-heated viewer in a warm climate with central AC, at replacement time, would be told both models say they rarely come out ahead when one says most do.
findings.suggestion: '...and even at replacement time the second model found gas homes rarely came out ahead, while the national lab model's winners were mostly warm-climate gas homes that already had central air.' At minimum, 'the second model found'.

findings.explanation: No double counting remains, but the contrast is not right for the national lab model. Its reference scenario replaces heating and cooling equipment at the same time (L429-L433; 'all heating and cooling equipment is replaced', L1269-L1272), so its 55% already is the furnace-and-air-conditioner-together case. Setting 'the case the national figures already describe' against 'replacing a failed furnace and air conditioner together' tells the viewer the about-a-year result lies beyond the national figures, and leaves unexplained why the same timing gives about a year in one Minnesota cost example (a propane-backup system priced from a cost database, propane furnace baseline) but a lifetime gain for at most 55% of homes nationally (s58). Deetjen, by contrast, credits only the heater (L527-L531), so for it the both-together case is indeed better timing.
findings.suggestion: Scope the about-a-year result to the one Minnesota example and drop the implied contrast, e.g. 'Buying when the old equipment is due is the case the national figures already describe; in the Minnesota example, replacing a failed furnace and air conditioner together turned decades of payback into about a year, a much better result than the national averages for the same timing.'

findings.explanation: 'Already give the heat pump its best timing' is right for the national lab model, which replaces heating and cooling together (L1269-L1272), but not for Deetjen, which credits only the replacement of the existing heater (equation 3, L500-L506; replacement cost by heater fuel, L527-L531) and not an air conditioner due at the same time. The script's own field evidence (s34, s39) shows replacing both together is better timing than replacing the heater alone. s62's 'the good-timing case' is accurate; 'best' is stronger than one of the two passages.
findings.suggestion: 'Both of those national figures already assume good timing; the field data show what it costs to switch before the old equipment is due.'

findings.explanation: 'From decades' is loose for the no-failure paybacks in CEE's Table 11 (28.8 years against a condensing furnace but 14.5 against an 82% furnace); the exact figures are given in s33 ten sentences earlier, so the summary does not mislead, and 'about a year' fairly renders 0.6-1.1.
